summary: Pharaoh welcomes Joseph's family into Goshen, Jacob blesses him, and Joseph supplies the household with food. As famine exhausts the population's money and livestock, Joseph buys the Egyptians and their land for Pharaoh and institutes a continuing fifth-share levy, while Israel prospers; the aging Jacob then requires Joseph to swear that he will bury him with his ancestors outside Egypt.
whyItMatters: The chapter places a favored migrant household beside a population surrendering property and independence to survive. It also insists that security in Egypt does not erase Jacob's attachment to the ancestral burial place.

context.author: Genesis names no narrator or final compiler. Tradition associates the Torah with Moses; the history of its composition remains debated.
context.audience: Israel reflecting on its ancestral promises, family relationships, and arrival in Egypt. The chapter does not identify a more specific original audience.
context.date: The ancestral story is set earlier than the book’s final literary form. Its composition and editing developed over time, with exact dates and models debated.
context.setting: Pharaoh's court, Goshen, and Egypt's famine economy, ending seventeen years into Jacob's Egyptian residence.
context.literaryForm: Royal reception, famine administration account, an explanation of a continuing land levy, and a deathbed burial oath.

before.text: God has reassured Jacob about Egypt, the household has arrived, and Joseph has prepared his brothers to explain their shepherding occupation.

here.text: The family receives land and bread while Joseph's food policy transfers Egyptian resources to Pharaoh; Jacob's burial request then turns attention back toward Canaan.

after.text: When Jacob becomes ill, Joseph brings Ephraim and Manasseh for blessing, and Jacob connects their inheritance with God's promise of the ancestral land.

outline.heading: Brothers presented and settlement authorized
outline.note: The family seeks pasture, and Pharaoh grants Goshen and possible livestock responsibilities.

outline.heading: Jacob before Pharaoh and the family provided for
outline.note: Jacob describes his pilgrimage and blesses Pharaoh; Joseph supplies bread.

outline.heading: Money and livestock exchanged for food
outline.note: Famine transfers wealth to Pharaoh through Joseph’s administration.

outline.heading: People and land acquired for Pharaoh
outline.note: The Egyptians sell themselves and their fields, while priestly land is exempt.

outline.heading: Seed and a continuing fifth-share levy
outline.note: Four parts remain for households and seed while Pharaoh receives one fifth.

outline.heading: Israel’s growth and Jacob’s burial oath
outline.note: The family prospers, and Jacob asks to be carried to the ancestral burial place.

keyVerses.text: Why should we die before your eyes, both we and our land? Buy us and our land for bread, and we and our land will be servants to Pharaoh. Give us seed, that we may live, and not die, and that the land won’t be desolate.”
keyVerses.why: The Egyptians’ offer to sell themselves and their land arises from the threat of starvation.

keyVerses.text: Then Joseph said to the people, “Behold, I have bought you and your land today for Pharaoh. Behold, here is seed for you, and you shall sow the land.
keyVerses.why: Joseph explicitly says he has bought both the people and their land for Pharaoh.

keyVerses.text: but when I sleep with my fathers, you shall carry me out of Egypt, and bury me in their burying place.” Joseph said, “I will do as you have said.”
keyVerses.why: Jacob asks for burial with his ancestors rather than permanent burial in Egypt.

questions.question: How does Jacob describe his life before Pharaoh?
questions.answer: He calls its years a pilgrimage and says they have been few and evil compared with his fathers' lives. The answer conveys hardship and transience even though he now stands before a king under his son's protection.

questions.question: What does “pilgrimage” mean in Jacob’s answer?
questions.answer: It presents his life as a course of sojourning rather than settled possession. In this context it describes his lived years and those of his ancestors, not a specific journey to a later religious shrine.

questions.question: What is the sequence of Egyptian losses?
questions.answer: The people first spend their money on grain, then exchange livestock for bread, and finally offer their bodies and land when nothing else remains. The progression shows how prolonged scarcity leaves them with fewer choices at every stage.

questions.question: Is the surrender of land and persons an ordinary freely chosen sale?
questions.answer: The Egyptians propose it while asking why they should die of hunger, and the narrator says the famine forces land sales. Their initiative and later gratitude coexist with desperate constraint; calling the exchange voluntary without that pressure would obscure the scene.

questions.question: Does the text say only land was bought?
questions.answer: No. Joseph tells the people he has bought both them and their land for Pharaoh, and they call themselves Pharaoh's servants. The chapter also reports relocation to cities in this WEB edition, so its account includes control over people as well as property.

questions.question: Why do the priests keep their land?
questions.answer: They receive a portion directly from Pharaoh and therefore do not need to sell their fields for food. The exception shows that access to royal support changes who bears the cost of the crisis.

questions.question: What are the continuing terms after seed is supplied?
questions.answer: One fifth of the harvest goes to Pharaoh, while four parts support seed, the workers, their households, and their children. The narrator presents this as a lasting statute and records the people's gratitude for survival without undoing the transfer of ownership.

questions.question: How does Israel’s situation compare with the wider population?
questions.answer: Israel acquires possessions and multiplies in Goshen while the preceding account describes Egyptian dispossession. The contrast is part of the chapter's arrangement and should remain visible alongside Joseph's care for his own family.

questions.question: Why does Jacob insist on an oath about burial?
questions.answer: He asks Joseph to deal kindly and truly with him by carrying him from Egypt to his fathers' burial place. The sworn request makes the ancestral connection concrete at the end of a life now materially settled in Egypt.

glossary.def: The one-fifth share of the harvest assigned to Pharaoh under Joseph’s statute.
Jacob’s description of the years of his life as a sojourner.
The Egyptians’ description of their resulting dependence on Pharaoh after Joseph buys them and their land.
